SPECIES.COMMENTS: Male----White males with elongated central tail feathers made a spectacular sight as they flew from tree to tree. Two races occur in Sri Lanka. The resident form, T. p. ceylonensis, in which the underparts are largely white, darkening only on the upper breast, is endemic to the island. Most birds seen appeared to be of the nominate form which is a winter visitor to Sri Lanka from breeding areas in Central Asia and northern India. These birds show rather more sullied underparts, and lack the white belly of the endemic form. Also, males of the endemic form apparently never attain the white plumage, so all those stunningly beautiful white males seen were of the nominate form.

SPECIES.COMMENTS: A fully white male with long tail streamers.----An overwintering migrant.----Habitat. Next to a rubber tree grove. A small cave-like open patch of space covered by lianas. ----Behaviour: The individual was vigorously giving  frequent calls in rapid-burst non-stop and flitting about amidst a backdrop of red-vented bulbuls calling loudly and vigorously. For context, usually an individual may call once and wait a couple of seconds before giving the next call during a normal day-time behaviour such as sallying for insects.----Audio attached is: Calls of red-vented bulbuls interspersed with the call of the one Indian paradise flycatcher.----This must be the roosting call of the species: a series of calls repeated in close succession in a roosting place, which is a place to settle and rest for the night.----Time observed: 5.45 p.m.----Given the vigorous interspecific nature of this interaction my best guess is the flycatcher is announcing its claim in this roosting territory for the night to the other birds, the bulbuls(who were also vigorously calling).----or it may serve another communicative purpose.
STATE.NAME: Sri Lanka

SPECIES.COMMENTS: One white male was observed to have landed in the water in the middle of the Pushkarini, with its wings and tail spread out. It managed to propel itself over water and landed towards the edge of the Pushkarini, but was not able to get out of water. Later it was seen shivering, with its quivering wings  making ripples in water. after about 15 minutes it was seen with its eyes closed and still shivering. The bird was rescued from water later and was found to be completely soaked. It was wrapped in an hand kerchief and was placed on a stone surface in open sunlight and was allowed to dry. 10 minutes later, it was able fly short distance. As a few Bonnet Macaque were drawn towards the bird, the bird was picked-up again and released into thick vegetation some distance away. Its mouth, when open was observed to be light slimy-olive-green in colour.----The birds seen included White males-2, female-1

The wing & tail feathers were more like cinnamon - everything fits as an IPF.--4. Soon after moving onto the same direction, another bird flew away, which had totally rufous/rusty/cinnamon colored upper body like the male IPF (everything same, sans the tail). This might be the female. Saw just once, flying away... This might be the female Paradise Flycatcher.

A  male rufous upperparts with short tail (No tail streamer).--                Male: identified by the clear boundary of black vs. greyish white between the head and throat respectively.    --                Immature(Yearling)--                Don’t know how  if it is a resident or a wintering migrant from Indian or a locally migrating individual.----Specific locations the rufous short tailed spotted within the larger habitat: --6.765351047298144, 79.93943150011296--6.764872886479827, 79.93982375737113--------2. A (migrating) male with a WHITE tail streamer and streaks of white plumage among the majorly rufous/cinnamon upperparts.--                Male: because only males develop long tail streamers.--                An overwintering individual from India(the resident race T. p. ceylonensis  doesnt morph into white.)--                An adult, likely older than 2 or 3 years (multiple overwintering periods) --                An intermediate plumage-bearing individual most likely in the process of morphing into fully white plumage in the next few years.--   Specific locations the intermediate morph was spotted in: --6.764173138094811, 79.94088308685843--6.764788916726467, 79.93977443160595------Behaviour common to both individuals: --Calling using the distinctive rasping call. Restlessly flitting about in the same tree or flying away to another.----Habitat: A shared territory of a well shaded wooded patch next to a small lane.------*color named rufous can be also more accurately introduced as cinnamon.
